args.text: Utterson comes home in low spirits and studies Jekyll's will in his business room.
The will leaves all Jekyll's possessions to Edward Hyde, and Hyde inherits if Jekyll vanishes.
Utterson calls the will madness and now fears it is disgrace.
Utterson goes to Cavendish Square to consult his friend Dr. Lanyon.
Lanyon welcomes Utterson warmly as an old school and college friend.
Utterson asks whether he and Lanyon are Jekyll's two oldest friends.
Lanyon says Jekyll became too fanciful and wrong in mind over ten years ago.
Utterson asks Lanyon about Hyde, and Lanyon has never heard of him.
Utterson lies awake all night, haunted by Enfield's tale and the faceless figure.
Utterson resolves to hunt for Hyde, thinking 'If he be Mr. Hyde, I shall be Mr. Seek.'
Utterson keeps watch by the by-street door at all hours until his patience is rewarded.
A small plainly dressed man approaches the door with a key, and Utterson accosts him as Mr. Hyde.
Utterson accosts Hyde and asks to be admitted to see Jekyll.
Hyde tells Utterson that Dr. Jekyll is from home.
Utterson asks to see Hyde's face and studies it.
Hyde gives Utterson his address in Soho.
Hyde angrily accuses Utterson of lying about Jekyll's description.
Hyde snarls, unlocks the door, and disappears into the house.
Utterson walks away deeply disturbed by Hyde's appearance.
Utterson arrives at Jekyll's house and is admitted by Poole.
Poole tells Utterson that Dr. Jekyll has gone out.
Poole confirms Hyde has a key and comes by the dissecting room door.
Poole says all servants have orders to obey Hyde.
Poole says Hyde never dines there and mostly uses the laboratory.
Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.
